This guide goes with the Discover Coding tutorials (T0 to T4, and the reference sheets S1 to S9 and C1 to C10). Read Chapters 1 to 3 first to learn how a block program is built. How to use this guide

Every program in this kit has the same shape: sense a sensor, decide with an if-block, act on an output, then wait a moment. When something does not work, test each of those stages on its own and write the values to the serial port.

What the parts look like

Most parts come mounted in a 3D-printed housing with LEGO studs, so they clip straight onto the LEGO base. The housing colour tells the station apart: red for the sensors, black for the LED Bar, blue for the matrix, white for the 360° servo and brown for the 180° servo.

Chapter 1 · DiscoveringSet-up · 20 min

Discovering the board and the Vittascience interface

Your mission

Get the board talking to the laptop. By the end of this chapter you can plug in a module, open the Vittascience interface in Chrome, upload a program and read what the board says in the serial console.

1The ST NUCLEO-WB55 board

The ST NUCLEO-WB55 is a board made by STMicroelectronics. It carries an STM32 microcontroller: a small computer on one chip that runs a single program over and over. You can program it in Python or in blocks with the Vittascience interface.

In the kit, the board already has a blue Grove shield fitted on top. The shield offers sockets labelled D2, D3, D4, D5, D6, D8, several I²C sockets and a few analog (A) sockets. Grove modules plug into these sockets with a four-wire cable: no soldering and no loose wires.

The board also has three LEDs of its own, LED1 (blue), LED2 (green) and LED3 (red), and push buttons SW1, SW2 and SW3, so you can test a program before plugging anything in.

2Prepare the hardware

  1. Set the shield to 5V
    Find the small VCC switch on the Grove shield and slide it to 5V. The Ultrasonic Ranger and the LED Bar need 5V.
  2. Plug in the modules
    Use the standard ports from Chapter 4: Buzzer on D4, Ultrasonic Ranger on D2, LED Bar on D8, and so on. Grove cables only fit one way round.
  3. Connect the USB cable
    Into the port labelled CN1 on the Nucleo, then into the laptop. A red/green power light turns on.

3The Vittascience interface

In Google Chrome, go to en.vittascience.com/wb55. The interface talks to the board through the browser's serial-port feature, which Chrome and Edge have but Safari and Firefox do not. The page is laid out like this:

  • Top left: New project, Open existing project, Share project, Undo, Redo.
  • Left column, the block rack: a Search a block box, then the categories Display · Input/Output · Communication · Sensors · Actuators · Robots · AI › Cameras, a divider, then Logic · Loops · Math · Text · Variables · Lists · Functions · Exceptions. Click a category to open its drawer of blocks.
  • Centre, the workspace: where you snap blocks together. A new project already contains two blocks: On start (runs once) and Forever (repeats). You build every program by snapping blocks into them.
  • Top centre: the Upload button, with a ▾ menu holding Download .py, Download .bin and Disconnect.
  • Top right: full screen, settings, the three views (Block mode, Mixed mode, Code mode) and a ▶ Run on simulator button.
  • Bottom, the serial console: text sent back by the board, a box to send a message to the board, and Export, Variables, Files and REPL.

Work in Mixed mode: blocks on the left, the Python generated from them on the right, updating as you build. It is a good way to see what each block really does.

4Upload a program

  1. Click Upload
    The first time, Chrome lists the serial ports. Pick STMicroelectronics STLink Virtual COM Port and click Connect.
  2. Watch the board restart
    The program is sent, the board restarts and runs it straight away. Whatever the program writes to the serial port appears in the console, and so do error messages.
  3. Keep your work
    Share project gives you a link; Upload ▾ → Download .py saves the Python file. The finished tutorial programs are supplied as SITCC2026_[ID]_[Title].py files; load them with Open existing project.
Important information

If Upload does nothing, press the black RESET button on the Nucleo, choose Upload ▾ → Disconnect, then Upload again. Unplug the AI camera's I²C cable while uploading. If the console says "you must first flash the MicroPython firmware", ask a facilitator: the file is under Upload ▾ → Download .bin and is copied onto the NODE_WB55 drive that appears when the board is plugged in.

Chapter 2 · First programBeginner · 20 min

A first program: blink LED1

Your mission

Make the blue LED on the Nucleo blink. No module needed. On the way you meet the three ideas almost every program in this kit is built from: a loop, an output block and a wait.

1How the block pictures work

The block pictures in this guide are the real blocks, exported straight from the Vittascience interface, so they look exactly like what you will build. A white oval is a number or text you type; a box with a small ▾ arrow is a drop-down you choose from. Blocks drawn inside another block run inside it.

DisplayInput/OutputCommunicationSensorsActuatorsAI › CamerasLogicLoopsMathVariablesFunctions

2Build the software

  1. New project
    The workspace already has a Forever block (category Loops). Everything inside it repeats until the board is unplugged.
  2. Turn the LED on
    From Display, drag control [LED1 (blue)] LED to state [HIGH (1)] into the Forever block.
  3. Wait
    From Input/Output, drag wait (1) [second(s)] underneath. Type 500 and set the drop-down to millisecond(s).
  4. Turn it off and wait again
    Add a second control LED block set to LOW (0), then another wait 500 millisecond(s).
  5. Upload
    LED1 blinks on and off every half second.

Program 2.1 · Blink. In Mixed mode, Python like while True: and time.sleep_ms(500) appears on the right.

11 lines · open it with Open existing project

Simulator check: Simulator board module "LED Bleue" switches ON/OFF every 500 ms.

Python generated by Vittascience
import machine
import pyb
import utime

led1_blue = pyb.LED(3)

while True:
  led1_blue.on()
  utime.sleep_ms(500)
  led1_blue.off()
  utime.sleep_ms(500)

3Run and have fun!

★★★Change both waits to 100 ms. What happens?
★★★Make the on-time 100 ms and the off-time 900 ms: a short flash, long gap, like a heartbeat. Then swap LED1 for LED2 (green) or LED3 (red).
★★★Replace the two control blocks and one wait with a single toggle state of [LED1 (blue)] (also in Display). Same blink, half the blocks.
What you learned

The Forever loop, an output block, and timing with wait. Add a sensor and a decision and you have almost every program in this kit.

Chapter 3 · Building blocksBeginner → Intermediate · 45 min

The building blocks of a program

Your mission

Learn the handful of block types every tutorial uses: loops and waits, the serial console, variables, if/else, maths and functions. Once you know these you can read any program in the kit.

1Loops and waiting

Already in every new projectOn start runs the blocks inside it once, when the board powers up. That is where set-up goes: starting values of variables, a welcome message, a servo in its centre position. It cannot be deleted.
Already in every new projectForever repeats everything inside it, for ever, after On start has finished. This is the main loop: reading sensors, deciding, acting, again and again.

Input/Output		Pauses the program. Units: second(s), millisecond(s), microsecond(s). While waiting, the board does nothing else.

Input/Output		Stops here until the condition is true. The simplest way to make one button press count once.

Loops		Runs the blocks inside a fixed number of times.

Loops		Keeps looping while (or, from the drop-down, until) a condition is true.

Loops		A counting loop: i takes each value in turn. Fills the LED Bar segment by segment, sweeps a servo…

Input/Output		A stopwatch. Start it, then read how much time has passed, without blocking the loop with a wait.

2Seeing what the board sees

There is no block called "print". The block that sends text or a number to the serial console is write on serial port, in Communication. Use it early and often: it is the quickest way to find out why a program is not doing what you expect.

Program 3.1 · Print the distance five times a second. Drop the sensor block into the white slot in place of the default “Hello !”.

29 lines · open it with Open existing project

Simulator check: Console prints the Rangefinder value (1.51 cm at the default slider) five times a second.

Python generated by Vittascience
import machine
import utime

# Ultrasonic on D2
d2 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D2', machine.Pin.OUT)

def grove_getUltrasonicData(pin, data=&#x27;distance', timeout_us=30000):
  pin.init(machine.Pin.OUT)
  pin.off()
  utime.sleep_us(2)
  pin.on()
  utime.sleep_us(10)
  pin.off()
  pin.init(machine.Pin.IN)
  duration = machine.time_pulse_us(pin, 1, timeout_us)/1e6 # t_echo in seconds
  if duration > 0:
    if data == &#x27;distance':
      #sound speed, round-trip/2, get in cm
      return 343 * duration/2 * 100
    elif data == &#x27;duration':
      return duration
    else:
      raise ValueError("Data option &#x27;" + data + "' is not valid")
  else:
    return -1

while True:
  print(str(grove_getUltrasonicData(d2, data=&#x27;distance')))
  utime.sleep_ms(200)
  • Communication also has write graph, which plots a value live in the console's graph tab. Try it with the distance sensor.

3Variables: remembering a value

A variable is a named box that holds a value. In Variables, click Create variable and name it, say, dist or count. The drawer then offers set [dist] to, change [dist] by and the round [dist] block that reads it. Starting values (for example count = 0) go inside On start, so they are set once and not reset on every loop.

Program 3.2 · Read the sensor once per loop into a variable, then use the variable. Every decision in the loop then uses the same number.

4Decisions: if / else

In Logic, if … then runs its contents only when the condition is true; the drawer also has a ready-made if … then … else. Conditions are built with the compare block (= ≠ < ≤ > ≥) and joined with and, or, not.

Program 3.3 · A threshold decision: beep when something is closer than 30 cm.

51 lines · open it with Open existing project

Simulator check: Rangefinder at 60 cm: buzzer OFF. At 15 cm: buzzer 784 Hz.

Python generated by Vittascience
import machine
import utime
import pyb

# Ultrasonic on D2
d2 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D2', machine.Pin.OUT)
# Buzzer on D4
d4 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D4', machine.Pin.OUT)
led1_blue = pyb.LED(3)

def grove_getUltrasonicData(pin, data=&#x27;distance', timeout_us=30000):
  pin.init(machine.Pin.OUT)
  pin.off()
  utime.sleep_us(2)
  pin.on()
  utime.sleep_us(10)
  pin.off()
  pin.init(machine.Pin.IN)
  duration = machine.time_pulse_us(pin, 1, timeout_us)/1e6 # t_echo in seconds
  if duration > 0:
    if data == &#x27;distance':
      #sound speed, round-trip/2, get in cm
      return 343 * duration/2 * 100
    elif data == &#x27;duration':
      return duration
    else:
      raise ValueError("Data option &#x27;" + data + "' is not valid")
  else:
    return -1

def pitch (pin, noteFrequency, noteDuration, silence_ms = 10):
  if noteFrequency is not 0:
    microsecondsPerWave = 1e6 / noteFrequency
    millisecondsPerCycle = 1000 / (microsecondsPerWave * 2)
    loopTime = noteDuration * millisecondsPerCycle
    for x in range(loopTime):
      pin.high()
      utime.sleep_us(int(microsecondsPerWave))
      pin.low()
      utime.sleep_us(int(microsecondsPerWave))
  else:
    utime.sleep_ms(noteDuration)
  utime.sleep_ms(silence_ms)

while True:
  dist = grove_getUltrasonicData(d2, data=&#x27;distance')
  if dist < 30:
    pitch(d4, 784, 100)
  else:
    led1_blue.off()
  utime.sleep_ms(100)
  • For the Nucleo's own buttons, Input/Output has an event block, on switch button [SW1] [pressed] then …, which runs its contents on each press without you testing the button in the loop.

5Maths: turning one number into another

Arithmetic: + − × ÷ ^. Example: 10 − dist ÷ 10 turns 0–100 cm into 10–0 bars.
A whole number, for the LED Bar level. Drop-down: round, round up, round down.
Keeps a value in a safe range (0–10 for the bar, −75 to 75 for the servo).
Games, such as the robot's move in rock-paper-scissors.
Rescales a reading from one range to another: the "map" block.
Modulo. "Every 5th loop", or wrapping a counter.

6Functions: name a group of blocks

In Functions, drag define (function_name) onto the workspace and rename it chime. Put the three buzzer notes inside. The Functions drawer then offers a teal call block named chime that you can drop anywhere, for example inside Forever.

Program 3.4 · A G–E–C chime as a function, called from the Forever loop every 3 s with the teal chime call block.

28 lines · open it with Open existing project

Simulator check: Buzzer plays 784 → 659 → 523 Hz every 3 s.

Python generated by Vittascience
import machine
import utime

# Buzzer on D4
d4 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D4', machine.Pin.OUT)

def pitch (pin, noteFrequency, noteDuration, silence_ms = 10):
  if noteFrequency is not 0:
    microsecondsPerWave = 1e6 / noteFrequency
    millisecondsPerCycle = 1000 / (microsecondsPerWave * 2)
    loopTime = noteDuration * millisecondsPerCycle
    for x in range(loopTime):
      pin.high()
      utime.sleep_us(int(microsecondsPerWave))
      pin.low()
      utime.sleep_us(int(microsecondsPerWave))
  else:
    utime.sleep_ms(noteDuration)
  utime.sleep_ms(silence_ms)

def chime():
  pitch(d4, 784, 150)
  pitch(d4, 659, 150)
  pitch(d4, 523, 300)

while True:
  chime()
  utime.sleep(3)
Pitfall

If a function must change a variable of the main program (for example count), put a global variable [count] block (Variables) at the top of the function. Without it Python makes a separate local copy and the main program never sees the change. And never delete the Forever block: without it the generated Python has no import machine and stops at once with a NameError.

7Sense, decide, act

How your program thinks
  1. Sense: read a sensor into a variable (distance, switch, temperature, camera class).
  2. Decide: compare it with a threshold using if / else.
  3. Act: change an output (LED, buzzer, bar, servo, matrix).
  4. Wait: a short pause so the loop does not run thousands of times a second.

When something does not work, test each stage on its own: write the sensor value to the serial port, then the decision (true/false), then test the output with a fixed value.

Chapter 4 · WiringReference

Wiring rules and the standard port map

Every tutorial uses the same ports so programs can be shared between teams and stations.

1Golden rules

  • Each team gets one kit box. Check every part before starting; return each part to the same box at the end.
  • Use the standard ports below in every tutorial.
  • Only the servo port (D5) is a hard rule. The reason is in the interface itself: the Servomotor block's pin drop-down offers only D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12 (the PWM-capable pins), and D5 is the one with a free Grove socket on our shield.
  • Plug and unplug modules with the board powered off (USB cable out) when you can.
  • When debugging, change one thing at a time.

2Standard port map

PartPort(s)Direction / typeBlock rack category
Nucleo board: LED1 (blue), LED2 (green), LED3 (red), SW1, SW2Built inOutput (LEDs) / input (switches)Display, Input/Output
Grove Micro SwitchD3Digital input (0 or 1)Input/Output
Grove Ultrasonic RangerD2Distance input (cm)Sensors
Grove DHT11 Temperature & HumidityD2Temperature (°C) and humidity (%) inputSensors
Grove BuzzerD4Sound outputActuators
Grove LED Bar v2.0D8 (uses D8 and D9)Level output (0–10)Display
180° servo "180 · S"D5 onlyAngle output (−90° to +90°)Actuators
360° servo "360 · C"D5 onlySpeed and direction outputActuators
Grove 8×8 RGB LED MatrixAny I²C port64-colour picture outputDisplay
AI camera unit (Wio Lite AI)Any I²C port + its own USB-C powerClass number inputAI › Cameras
Link cableD6 on both boards (yellow = D6, white = D7)Output on sender, input on receiverInput/Output
Watch out

The Ultrasonic Ranger and the DHT11 both use D2; no tutorial uses both at once (Station S: Ranger, Station C: DHT11). And every pin drop-down defaults to D0 (D2/D3 for the LED Bar), so set it to the standard port each time you drag in a new block.

3Servo wiring

Both servos connect to D5 through the Grove-to-servo lead. Match the colours:

  • servo yellow → lead orange (signal)
  • servo red → lead red (+5V)
  • servo black → lead brown (GND)

The two servos look alike, so read the label: 180 · S is the position servo, 360 · C the continuous one.

Parts manual · 5.1

Nucleo board: LED1, LED2, LED3, SW1, SW2

Port
Built in (no cable)
Type
Input and output

The Nucleo has its own lights and buttons, so you can test a program before plugging anything in. LED1 is blue, LED2 green, LED3 red. SW1 and SW2 are the small push buttons on the board itself.

Blocks to use

Display		Turns an LED on (HIGH) or off (LOW). LED2 (green) and LED3 (red) are in the list.
Display		Flips the LED: on becomes off, off becomes on.
Input/Output		Gives 0 while the button is pressed and 1 when let go.
Input/Output		An event: runs its contents each time the button is pressed (or released).

Examples

Good to know

  • Pressed = 0 for SW1 and SW2. This catches many people out! The Grove Micro Switch is the other way round.
  • Use a "wait until" block after a press, or the "on switch button" event, so one press is counted only once.

Parts manual · 5.2

Grove Micro Switch

Port
D3
Type
Digital input (0 or 1)

A small lever switch. It reads 1 when pressed and 0 when released. In the station story it is the "doors open" sensor: mount it so the LEGO door or a minifigure pushes the lever.

Blocks to use

Input/Output		Gives 1 while the lever is pressed, 0 otherwise. The block defaults to D0: set D3.

Examples

Good to know

  • The switch reads 1 when pressed.
  • It bounces: one press can read as several. Wait about 30 ms, then "wait until" it is released before counting the next one.

Parts manual · 5.3

Grove Ultrasonic Ranger

Port
D2
Type
Distance input, in cm (about 3 to 350 cm)

It sends a click of sound too high to hear and times the echo. Point it straight at a flat, hard target.

Blocks to use

Sensors		Four drop-downs: sensor type (keep Grove), data (distance (cm) or round-trip duration (µs)), and pin (defaults to D0: set D2). Returns cm, or −1 when nothing is in range.

Examples

Good to know

  • It returns −1 when out of range, which a formula would take for "very close". Add the "if dist < 0 then set dist to 400" check right after reading.
  • Wait at least 50 ms between readings. Average three readings for a steadier value.
  • Soft or slanted surfaces reflect poorly, and the beam is wide: keep LEGO walls out of its path. Calibrate against a ruler (error = sensor − ruler).

Parts manual · 5.4

Grove DHT11 Temperature & Humidity

Port
D2
Type
Temperature (°C, 0–50, ±2) and relative humidity (%, 20–90, ±5) input

Two readings from one module. It is slow: read it at most once every 1 to 2 seconds.

Blocks to use

Sensors		Temperature. Unit drop-down: (°C), (°F), (K). Pin defaults to D0: set D2.
Sensors		Relative humidity (the block calls it "Moisture"). Same block, data drop-down changed.

Examples

Good to know

  • Read it at most once every 1–2 s; faster reads give stale or failed values.
  • To test it, breathe gently on it: humidity jumps, temperature creeps up.
  • It shares D2 with the Ultrasonic Ranger: only one of them is plugged in at a time.

Parts manual · 5.5

Grove Buzzer

Port
D4
Type
Sound output

Plays one tone at a time, at the frequency you choose, for a duration in milliseconds. Higher frequency = higher note.

Blocks to use

Actuators		One note: frequency in Hz, length in ms. Pin defaults to D0: set D4.
Actuators		A tune: a list of note blocks (C to B and Silence, octave 1–8, duration 1–8).
Actuators		Silence.
NoteCDEFGA
Frequency (Hz), octave 5523587659698784880

Examples

Good to know

  • A program with no Forever block does not work: Vittascience only adds import machine when a Forever block is present, so a run-once program stops with NameError: name 'machine' is not defined. Keep the Forever block even if it stays empty: put your set-up blocks in On start above it (Example 1).
  • The program waits while a note plays. Inside a loop that also reads a sensor, keep notes short (100–150 ms).
  • Put your chime in a function so you can reuse it.

Parts manual · 5.6

Grove LED Bar v2.0

Port
D8 (uses D8 and D9)
Type
Level output, 0 to 10 segments

Ten segments (8 green, 1 yellow, 1 red). One Grove cable in D8 carries both the data (D8) and the clock (D9).

Blocks to use

Display		Lights that many segments. The block defaults to DI D2 / DCKI D3: change both to D8 and D9. (LED Bar Module invert display fills it from the other end.)

Examples

Good to know

  • When the level comes from a calculation, wrap it in round, e.g. round(10 − dist ÷ 10), and keep it between 0 and 10 with constrain.
  • Write the level to the serial port too, so you can see the number the bar is given.

Parts manual · 5.7

180° servo, label "180 · S"

Port
D5 only, through the Grove-to-servo lead
Type
Angle output, −90° to +90°, 0° = centre

A position servo: give it an angle and it moves there and holds. Wiring: servo yellow → lead orange (signal), red → red (+5V), black → brown (GND).

Blocks to use

Actuators		Moves to the angle. The pin list offers only D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12 and defaults to D3: set D5. The default angle is 90: type over it.

Examples

Good to know

  • Find the safe range first (try −75° and +75°). Fit the arrow after moving to 0°, so centre is centre.
  • If it buzzes or strains, the angle is beyond its range or the horn is blocked. Back off at once: a straining servo can reset the board.

Parts manual · 5.8

360° servo, label "360 · C"

Port
D5 only, through the Grove-to-servo lead
Type
Speed (0–100 %) and direction output

A continuous-rotation servo: give it a speed and a direction and it keeps turning until you set speed 0. It cannot go to an angle. Same lead and wiring as the 180° servo.

Blocks to use

Actuators		Direction ↺ or ↻. Pin list D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12 (defaults to D3: set D5).

Examples

Good to know

  • Speed 0 stops it. Test 10, 20, 50 and 100 % in both directions; below about 5 % it does not turn.
  • Keep a "speed 0" block somewhere reachable, or the servo keeps turning after your loop ends.
  • Do not mix up the servos: an angle sent to the 360 makes it spin; a speed sent to the 180 makes it jump to one end.

Parts manual · 5.9

Grove 8×8 RGB LED Matrix

Port
Any I²C port
Type
64-colour picture output

64 colour LEDs in an 8×8 grid. You paint the picture in the 8×8 editor built into the block (the default is a white smiley).

Blocks to use

Display		Shows the picture painted in the block's grid. Take the RGB LED Matrix block, not the single-colour LED Matrix just above it.
Display		Turns all 64 LEDs off.

Examples

Good to know

  • Draw icons bold (2-pixel lines) so they read from across the room. Right-click a display block → Duplicate to reuse a picture.
  • If the AI camera is also on I²C, unplug the camera's cable while uploading, then plug it back in.

Parts manual · 5.10

AI camera unit (Wio Lite AI)

Port
Any I²C port, plus its own USB-C power
Type
Class number input (1, 2, 3 … in training order)

A small camera with its own processor. You train it at en.vittascience.com/ia/images on pictures of your own categories, export the model to the camera, and the Nucleo asks it which category it sees. Class 1 is the first category you created, 2 the second, and so on.

Blocks to use

AI › Cameras		Asks the camera to look and decide. Call it before every read.
AI › Cameras		The class number the camera chose.
AI › Cameras		How sure it is (0–1) about class n. retrieve all data gives them all.
AI › Cameras		Checks the camera is alive (status / version).

Examples

Train, export, use

  1. Train
    On the AI interface, create one category per thing to recognise, add 20–40 images each (vary angle and distance), click Train the model and check the preview. Add images where it is unsure.
  2. Export
    Click the Microcontroller button, connect the camera by USB-C and follow the steps on screen. Note the category order: class 1 is the first you created.
  3. Use
    Plug the camera's I²C cable into the shield, keep it powered by USB-C, and upload your Nucleo program with the I²C cable unplugged during the upload.

Good to know

  • Always launch a prediction before reading detected class ID, or you read the old answer.
  • The Grove I²C cable only carries data; the camera needs its own USB-C power. Keep the lighting as it was when you trained.
  • Unplug the I²C cable while uploading, reconnect, then press RESET. If the live prediction freezes, press the reset button on the Wio Lite board.
  • If the result flickers between two classes, act only after three identical results (Example 2).

Parts manual · 5.11

Link cable
D6 ↔ D6

Link cable between two stations

Port
D6 on both boards (yellow wire = D6, white wire = D7)
Type
Output on the sending board, input on the receiving board. Two wires carry four codes (0–3).

A Grove cable prepared by the facilitators with the red (VCC) wire cut. Each board keeps its own USB power; the cable shares only ground and the two signals.

Blocks to use

Input/Output		Sender: sets D6 or D7 high (1) or low (0).
Input/Output		Receiver: reads D6 or D7.
Value to sendD7D6Code
0 / nothing000
1011
2102
3113

Examples

Good to know

  • Use only the facilitator's link cable, with the red wire cut. A normal Grove cable would join the 5V rails of two separately powered boards.
  • Test the receiver alone first: Micro Switch on D6 (code 1), then on D7 (code 2). Agree the code table with the other station.

Chapter 6 · Applications5 projects · Beginner → Intermediate

Example applications

Five small applications, each adding one idea. Build them in order: each is the seed of a Discover Coding tutorial.

1Boarding chime → T1 / S1

Parts: Buzzer on D4. Idea: a sequence of outputs and timing.

This is Program 3.4 (download it in Chapter 3 §6). Challenge: add a fourth note, then play the chime only when SW1 is pressed (try the on switch button block).

2Crowd meter → S2

Parts: LED Bar on D8. Idea: variables and counting.

24 lines · open it with Open existing project

Simulator check: Three SW1 presses: LED Bar 3.

Python generated by Vittascience
import machine
import pyb
from stm32_my9221 import MY9221
import utime

sw1 = pyb.Pin(&#x27;SW1')
sw1.init(pyb.Pin.IN, pyb.Pin.PULL_UP, af=-1)
d8 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D8', machine.Pin.OUT)
d9 = machine.Pin(&#x27;D9', machine.Pin.OUT)
# LED Bar DI/DCKI on d8/d9
ledBar_d8 = MY9221(d8, d9)

crowd = 0

while True:
  while not (sw1.value() == 0):
    pass
  crowd = crowd + 1
  if crowd > 10:
    crowd = 0
  ledBar_d8.level(crowd)
  utime.sleep_ms(30)
  while not (sw1.value() == 1):
    pass

Each press of SW1 adds a passenger; past 10 the carriage empties. Challenge: use SW2 to remove a passenger.

3Doors open! → S3

Parts: Micro Switch on D3, LED Bar on D8, Buzzer on D4. Idea: if / else on a digital input. Use Example 2 of sheet 5.2. Challenge: chime once when the door opens, not continuously.

4Door-zone distance meter → T2 / S4

Parts: Ultrasonic Ranger on D2, LED Bar on D8, Buzzer on D4, ruler. Idea: mapping one range onto another, and calibration.

  1. Print the distance
    Every 0.2 s (Program 3.1). Move your hand closer and further away.
  2. Calibration lab
    Hold a book at 10, 20, 30, 50 and 80 cm. Write what the console says. Error = sensor − ruler.
  3. Distance to bars
    Closer = more bars. 100 cm or more = 0 bars, 0 cm = 10 bars. Formula: bars = 10 − dist ÷ 10 (Example 2 of sheet 5.3), or the Math transform the value block.
Do thisYou should see✓
Hand at 50 cmAbout 5 bars, no beep☐
Hand at 20 cmAbout 8 bars + beeping☐
Nothing in front0 bars, quiet☐
Calibration tableErrors within 1–2 cm☐
★★★Change the door zone to 20 cm. Which value feels right for your LEGO model?
★★★Make the beep faster the closer someone gets (wait time = dist × 5 ms).
★★★Mount the sensor in your LEGO platform, pointing across the door zone, and test it with a minifigure crowd.

5Pointer arrow → S5

Parts: 180° servo on D5, Micro Switch on D3. Idea: toggling a state with a variable. Use Example 2 of sheet 5.7. Challenge: sweep from −70° to +70° in 5° steps with count with i from −70 to 70 by step 5, then jump back.

Where next?

T3 (Boarding State Machine) combines all the Station S parts around a state variable (waiting → boarding → closing). T4 (Comfort Check) combines the camera, the matrix and the DHT11. The references S6–S9 and C1–C9 each add one more idea: see Chapter 8.

Chapter 7 · TestingReference

Testing and debugging

Debug like an engineer

Change ONE thing at a time. Test the part on its own (sensor, then decision, then output). Write values to the serial port so you can see what the board sees.

!Fix it

If this happens…Try this
Upload shows no serial port / does nothingUse Chrome. USB cable in CN1. Press RESET. Upload ▾ → Disconnect, then Upload again. Unplug the camera's I²C cable during upload.
Console says "you must first flash the MicroPython firmware"The board lost its firmware. Ask a facilitator; the file is under Upload ▾ → Download .bin.
Console says NameError: name 'machine' is not definedThere is no Forever block in the program. Vittascience adds import machine only when one exists. Add an empty Forever block under your blocks.
A "read digital pin" or "read state of switch" block will not snap into a maths blockThey give a true/false value and the maths slots only accept numbers. Put the reading into a variable first (set b7 to read digital pin D7), then use the variable in the maths. Comparisons (= 1) accept them directly.
Simulator shows AttributeError: '' object has no attribute 'writeto'The program uses the AI camera, which the simulator cannot imitate (I²C). The code is fine: test it on the real board.
Upload worked but nothing happensAre your blocks inside the Forever block? Blocks outside it run once at start and stop.
Console shows a red errorSwitch to Mixed mode and read the last line: it gives the Python line number. Usual causes: a variable used before it is set, text where a number is expected, or a function changing a variable without global variable.
A module does nothingCheck the pin drop-down matches the socket (new blocks default to D0!). VCC switch on 5V. Try another socket, changing the block to match.
Distance is always 0, −1 or hugeCheck D2. Nothing right up against the sensor. Add the "if dist < 0 then set dist to 400" fix.
Numbers jump aroundSoft things absorb sound: use a flat book, aim straight on. Average three readings; wait ≥ 50 ms between readings.
Bar shows nothing even when closePrint "bars" too. Is the formula 10 − dist ÷ 10, not dist ÷ 10 − 10? Rounded and between 0 and 10? DI/DCKI set to D8/D9?
One press counts as manySwitch bounce. Wait 30 ms, then wait until released.
Switch logic is backwardsMicro Switch = 1 when pressed; SW1/SW2 = 0 when pressed.
Servo block won't let me pick D4 or D8Correct: it offers only the PWM pins (D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12). Use D5.
Servo buzzes, jitters, or the board resetsAngle beyond the safe range, or the horn is blocked. Reduce the angle. Check lead colours (orange/red/brown) and that the lead is in D5.
360 servo won't startSpeed below ~5 %. Use 10 % or more.
Matrix blankI²C cable seated? Did you use RGB LED Matrix (not plain LED Matrix)? Anything painted in the grid? Camera unplugged during upload?
Camera always returns the same classlaunch a prediction before reading? Camera on USB-C power? Model exported? Try get the status. Lighting as in training?
Camera flickers between classesAct only after 3 identical results. Add training images near the boundary.
Buzzer makes the sensor "miss" thingsThe program waits while a note plays. Use 100–150 ms notes inside sensing loops.
Link cable gives wrong codesTest the receiver alone with the Micro Switch on D6, then D7. Same code table on both sides? Both boards on their own USB power?

Appendix BKey words

Key words

WordWhat it means
MicrocontrollerA small computer on one chip that runs one program for ever. The Nucleo WB55 is one.
GroveA plug-and-play system: modules with a 4-pin socket and a standard cable, no soldering.
Digital pinA connection that is either 0 (LOW, 0 V) or 1 (HIGH, 3.3 V). D2–D8 on the shield.
PWM pinA pin that can output a fast on/off signal to drive a servo or dim an LED. Only D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12 on this board.
I²CA two-wire bus that lets several smart modules (matrix, camera) share the same sockets.
Input / outputInput brings information in (switch, sensor). Output sends something out (LED, buzzer, servo).
Serial port / consoleThe USB link between board and laptop. "write on serial port" sends text to the console at the bottom of the interface.
LoopRepeating a set of blocks. "Forever" repeats until power off.
VariableA named box that stores a value you can change and read later.
ConditionA yes/no question such as "dist < 30", used by if, wait until and repeat while.
ThresholdA cut-off number, e.g. "closer than 30 cm".
MapChange a number from one range to another, e.g. 0–100 cm → 10–0 bars. In Vittascience the block is "transform the value".
CalibrationChecking a sensor against a real ruler (or thermometer) and recording the error.
DebounceIgnoring the rapid on/off flicker a switch makes when pressed, so one press counts once.
UltrasonicSound too high for humans to hear. The sensor times its echo to measure distance.
ServoA motor you command. 180° type goes to an angle; 360° type spins at a speed.
ClassA category the camera was trained to recognise, returned as a number.
State machineA program organised around a "state" variable (waiting, boarding, closing) with rules for moving between states.
UploadSending your program from Vittascience to the board over USB. The board restarts and runs it.
Mixed modeThe editor view with blocks on the left and the generated Python on the right.

Appendix CSimulator test log · 18 Oct 2026

Every program was built and run in the Vittascience simulator

All 28 programs in this guide were assembled as real blocks in the NUCLEO-WB55 interface at en.vittascience.com/wb55, converted to Python by the interface, and run with its ▶ Run on simulator button. Sensor inputs were driven with the simulator's own sliders. Each program's Complete program panel carries the result and a download of the .py project file, which re-opens as blocks with Open existing project.

Verified

24 programs ran and behaved as described. The 4 camera programs generate correct code but cannot run in the simulator, because the Wio Lite AI camera (an I²C device) is not simulated; they must be tested on the real board.

What the live interface taught us (now built into the guide)

  • Keep the Forever block. Without it the generated Python has no import machine and fails with NameError. Run-once examples now sit above an empty Forever block.
  • Readings are true/false, not numbers. read digital pin and read state of switch output a Boolean. They snap into comparison blocks (= 1) but not into + − × ÷. Store them in a variable first (the link-cable receiver was rewritten this way).
  • Servo pin list. The Servomotor blocks store the pin as a timer channel (D5 = TIM2_CH1); only D3, D5, D6, D9, D11, D12 are offered. Negative angles (−70°) are accepted and the simulator shows them.
  • Continuous servo below 5 %. The generated setServoSpeed sets the pulse to 0 for any speed under 5 %, which is why the servo "does not turn" there.
  • Camera reads take 1 s. The generated wio_get_class_data contains utime.sleep(1), so a camera loop runs at most once per second.
  • Simulator sliders. The Rangefinder slider is the echo time in µs (88 to 14575), not centimetres: 20 cm ≈ 1166 µs, 50 cm ≈ 2915 µs. SW1 is "1 = pressed" on the slider but the program reads 0 when pressed, as on the real board.
